what_its_for: Lorazepam is used to treat anxiety disorders and to provide short-term relief of anxiety symptoms. It may also be used to help with sleep problems related to anxiety, to prevent seizures, or to help you relax before a medical procedure. It belongs to a group of medicines called benzodiazepines, which work by calming your brain and nervous system.
how_to_take: Take lorazepam exactly as your doctor prescribed. You can take it with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Do not crush, chew, or break the tablet unless your doctor tells you to. Do not take more than your prescribed dose or take it more often than directed. This medicine can be habit-forming, so only use it for as long as your doctor recommends.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you based on your condition, age, and other health factors. For anxiety, adults are usually started on a low dose taken 2 to 3 times per day. The typical dose ranges from 0.5 mg to 2 mg per dose. For sleep problems, a single dose is usually taken at bedtime. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions. Never change your dose on your own without talking to your doctor first.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still several hours before your next scheduled dose. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one. If you are unsure what to do, call your pharmacist or doctor.
storage: Store lorazepam at room temperature, between 59°F and 77°F (15°C to 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Do not store it in the bathroom. Keep this medicine in a safe, secure place out of reach of children and pets. Do not share this medication with anyone else, as this is illegal and can be dangerous. Dispose of unused medication safely — ask your pharmacist about local drug take-back programs.
what_to_avoid: Do not drink alcohol while taking lorazepam. Alcohol can dangerously increase the effects of this medicine and may cause serious breathing problems or extreme drowsiness. Avoid driving, operating heavy machinery, or doing anything that requires you to be fully alert until you know how this medicine affects you. Avoid taking other medications that cause drowsiness, such as sleep aids, muscle relaxers, narcotic pain medicines, or other anxiety medications, unless your doctor approves. Do not stop taking lorazepam suddenly without talking to your doctor, as this can cause withdrawal symptoms.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the nearest emergency room if you experience: severe drowsiness or difficulty staying awake, slow, shallow, or troubled breathing, confusion or unusual changes in mood or behavior, thoughts of harming yourself, signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, swelling of the face or throat, or trouble breathing. Also contact your doctor if you feel the medication is not working, if you feel you need to take more than prescribed, or if you notice signs of dependence such as feeling like you cannot function without the medication.
when_it_works: Lorazepam works fairly quickly. You may start to feel calmer or more relaxed within 30 to 60 minutes after taking a dose. The effects usually last about 6 to 8 hours. It is meant for short-term use only, typically no longer than 2 to 4 weeks. Talk to your doctor about long-term treatment options for anxiety if you need ongoing help.
special_populations: Older adults (65 and older) are more sensitive to the effects of lorazepam and are at higher risk for falls, confusion, and memory problems. Lower doses are usually recommended for elderly patients. Lorazepam should NOT be used during pregnancy, as it can harm the unborn baby. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, tell your doctor before taking this medicine. It is also not recommended for children unless specifically prescribed by a specialist. If you have liver or kidney disease, breathing problems, a history of substance abuse, depression, or glaucoma, be sure to tell your doctor before starting this medication.
